terms.register: Cic. in epistulīs et ōrātiōnibus; Plaut.
evidence: Cic. Att. 1.18.5: ō dī immortālēs! quam ignāvus ac sine animō mīles!
terms.comment: Also with ō or prō before it. Cicero’s commonest exclamation.

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Plaut., Ter.; also Cic. (Imp. Pomp. 33, Lewis & Short)
evidence: Plaut. Curc. 274: Prō dī immortālēs, quem cōnspiciō? quis illic est?
terms.comment: Lewis & Short (s.v. prō interj.): “wonder or lamentation”.

terms.register: vōx sermōnis cotīdiānī: Cic. in epistulīs
evidence: Cic. Att. 14.9.2: ō dī bonī! vīvit tyrannis, tyrannus occidit!
Plaut. Amph. 1074: crēdō edepol, nam, prō Juppiter, sepultust quasi sit mortuos.

terms.register: vōx cōmica: Ter.; also Cic. (Tusc. 5.48, Lewis & Short)
evidence: Ter. And. 246: Prō deum atque hominum fidem!
terms.comment: An appeal to the protection of gods and men, said in outrage; for a real cry for help see help!.

terms.gloss: for heaven’s sake! (literally, I beg you)
terms.grammar: first person of obsecrāre, used as an interjection
evidence: Traupman 107: for heaven’s sake, obsecrō (lit. I pray)
terms.comment: An appeal or an exclamation of dismay; see also please.

terms.gloss: for heaven’s sake! in heaven’s name!

phrases.latin: Aulī autem fīlius, ō dī immortālēs! quam ignāvus ac sine animō mīles!
phrases.english: And Aulus’s son, good heavens! what a cowardly, spiritless soldier!

phrases.latin: Prō dī immortālēs, quem cōnspiciō? quis illic est?
phrases.english: Good heavens, who is that I see? who’s there?

phrases.latin: ō dī bonī! vīvit tyrannis, tyrannus occidit!
phrases.english: Good gods! the tyranny lives, the tyrant is dead!

phrases.latin: crēdō edepol, nam, prō Juppiter, sepultust quasi sit mortuos.
phrases.english: I believe it, by Pollux; for, good Lord, he’s buried as if he were dead.

sources: Lewis & Short: prō (interj.) · Lewis & Short: deus · Lewis & Short: Juppiter
